_note: Keyed by event year (negative = BC). confidence: high | medium | debated. Keep claims conservative; cite primary sources and note disagreements.

-605.summary: The battle of Carchemish and Nebuchadnezzar's accession are among the best-dated events of the period.

sources.name: Babylonian Chronicle (ABC 5, 'Chronicle of the Early Years of Nebuchadnezzar'), British Museum BM 21946
sources.note: Records the crown prince defeating the Egyptian army at Carchemish, Nabopolassar's death and Nebuchadnezzar's accession in 605 BC.

sources.name: Jeremiah 46:2
sources.note: Dates the Egyptian defeat at Carchemish to the 4th year of Jehoiakim.

sources.name: Excavations at Carchemish (Woolley, 1910s; Turco-Italian team, 2011–)
sources.note: Destruction layers and Egyptian-related finds consistent with a violent end c. 605 BC.

views: Daniel 1:1 dates a siege of Jerusalem to Jehoiakim's 3rd year; many scholars see a conflict with Jeremiah's dating, while others explain it by Babylonian accession-year reckoning.
The Chronicle does not name Daniel or a deportation in 605; that detail rests on the biblical text.

-586.summary: The Babylonian conquest of Judah is confirmed by chronicles, letters and archaeology. The exact year of the temple's destruction is debated (587 vs 586 BC).

sources.name: Babylonian Chronicle (ABC 5)
sources.note: Records the capture of 'the city of Judah' on 2 Adar, 597 BC and the appointment of a new king. The chronicle breaks off before 587/586.

sources.name: Lachish Letters (ostraca, c. 588–586 BC)
sources.note: Letter 4 says the writer can no longer see the signals of Azekah, which fits the final Babylonian campaign (cf. Jeremiah 34:7).

sources.name: Jerusalem burn layers (City of David, 'Burnt Room', 'House of Bullae')
sources.note: Destruction debris, arrowheads and clay seals from the early 6th century BC.

sources.name: Jehoiachin ration tablets (Babylon)
sources.note: List rations for 'Yaukin, king of Judah' in exile.

views: 587 BC vs 586 BC depends on how the regnal years of Zedekiah are reckoned.
Scholars debate the scale of the exile and how far the land was depopulated.

-539.summary: Babylon fell to Cyrus in October 539 BC. Babylonian and Persian sources agree that it was taken with little fighting.

sources.name: Nabonidus Chronicle (ABC 7), British Museum BM 35382
sources.note: Battle at Opis, then 'the army of Cyrus entered Babylon without battle' (16 Tashritu); Cyrus arrives days later.

sources.name: Cyrus Cylinder, British Museum BM 90920
sources.note: Persian royal propaganda that presents Cyrus as chosen by Marduk and describes the return of displaced gods and peoples.

sources.name: Herodotus 1.191; Xenophon, Cyropaedia 7.5
sources.note: Later Greek accounts of the city taken while the Euphrates was diverted and during a festival. Treated cautiously.

sources.name: Daniel 5
sources.note: Belshazzar's feast. Belshazzar is attested in cuneiform as Nabonidus's son and regent (Verse Account of Nabonidus; Nabonidus Cylinder).

views: Daniel 5:31's 'Darius the Mede' is not identified in extra-biblical sources. Proposals include Gubaru/Gobryas or Cyrus himself; many critical scholars see a literary figure.
The Cylinder does not mention Jews; linking it to Ezra 1 is plausible but indirect.
Traditional reading: the silver chest = Medo-Persia. Critical reading: Media and Persia are separate kingdoms (2nd and 3rd).

-334.summary: Alexander crossed the Hellespont in spring 334 BC and defeated the Persian satraps at the Granicus.

sources.name: Arrian, Anabasis 1.11–16
sources.note: The most detailed account, based on Ptolemy and Aristobulus (written c. AD 130–160).

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Alexander 16; Diodorus 17.19–21
sources.note: Differ on details such as timing (evening vs dawn attack).

views: All narrative accounts were written centuries later, using lost contemporary sources.
Troop numbers are uncertain and often inflated.

-333.summary: At Issus (November 333 BC), Alexander defeated Darius III in person. Darius fled, leaving his family behind.

sources.name: Arrian 2.6–12; Curtius Rufus 3.8–11; Plutarch, Alexander 20
sources.note: Agree on the outcome. They differ on numbers and on details of the battle.

sources.name: Alexander Mosaic, Pompeii (c. 100 BC, after an earlier Greek painting)
sources.note: Shows Alexander confronting Darius, probably at Issus or Gaugamela.

views: The exact battlefield river (Pinarus) is debated: the Payas or the Deli Çay.

-331.summary: Gaugamela (1 October 331 BC) broke the Achaemenid army. Babylon opened its gates to Alexander soon after.

sources.name: Babylonian Astronomical Diary (BM 36761 + 36390)
sources.note: A contemporary cuneiform record: a lunar eclipse 11 days before the battle, the defeat of Darius's army, and Alexander's entry into Babylon.

sources.name: Arrian 3.7–15; Plutarch, Alexander 31–33; Diodorus 17.56–61
sources.note: Narrative accounts of the battle.

views: The eclipse of 20 September 331 BC dates the battle firmly.
Traditional reading: the bronze belly = Greece/Alexander. In the critical four-kingdom scheme, Greece is the 4th (iron) kingdom.

-323.summary: Alexander died in Babylon in June 323 BC. His generals fought for decades; after Ipsus (301 BC) the empire settled into major successor kingdoms.

sources.name: Babylonian Astronomical Diary (BM 45962)
sources.note: Records 'the king died' on 29 Aiaru (10/11 June 323 BC).

sources.name: Arrian 7.24–28; Plutarch, Alexander 75–77; Diodorus 18–20
sources.note: Death narratives and the wars of the Diadochi.

views: Daniel 7:6 and 8:8, 8:22 describe four heads or horns. They are usually linked to Cassander, Lysimachus, Seleucus and Ptolemy after 301 BC; the split was gradual, not immediate.
The cause of death (fever, malaria, typhoid, poison) is still debated.

-168.summary: At Pydna (168 BC), Rome destroyed the Macedonian kingdom of Perseus. The same year, Rome forced Antiochus IV out of Egypt (the 'Day of Eleusis').

sources.name: Livy 44.36–42; Plutarch, Aemilius Paullus 16–22
sources.note: Accounts of the battle; Polybius (a contemporary) survives only in fragments.

sources.name: Pillar monument of Aemilius Paullus, Delphi
sources.note: A surviving victory monument with a relief of the battle.

sources.name: Polybius 29.27
sources.note: Popillius Laenas draws a circle around Antiochus IV. Often linked to Daniel 11:30 ('ships of Kittim').

views: Critical scholars date Daniel's final composition to c. 167–164 BC, under Antiochus IV. Traditional scholars hold a 6th-century authorship with predictive prophecy.

-63.summary: Pompey took Jerusalem in 63 BC and entered the Holy of Holies, ending Hasmonean independence.

sources.name: Josephus, Antiquities 14.4; Jewish War 1.7
sources.note: The siege, the entry into the sanctuary, and Pompey leaving the treasury untouched.

sources.name: Psalms of Solomon 2, 8, 17
sources.note: A near-contemporary Jewish response to the conquest.

sources.name: Cicero, Pro Flacco 67
sources.note: Mentions Pompey not touching the temple treasures.

views: Josephus wrote over a century later and relied partly on Nicolaus of Damascus and Strabo.

-30.summary: After Actium (31 BC), Octavian took Alexandria in 30 BC; Cleopatra VII died, and the last Hellenistic kingdom became a Roman province.

sources.name: Res Gestae Divi Augusti 27
sources.note: Augustus: 'I added Egypt to the empire of the Roman people.'

sources.name: Plutarch, Antony 76–86; Cassius Dio 51
sources.note: Narrative of the fall of Alexandria and Cleopatra's death.

sources.name: 'Aegypto capta' coinage (28 BC)
sources.note: Roman coins commemorating the capture of Egypt.

views: The asp story is reported by ancient writers but its details are uncertain.

70.summary: Titus's legions destroyed Jerusalem and the Second Temple in AD 70.

sources.name: Josephus, Jewish War 6
sources.note: An eyewitness account by a participant with the Roman side.

sources.name: Arch of Titus, Rome (c. AD 81)
sources.note: Relief of soldiers carrying the menorah and temple spoils in the triumph.

sources.name: Burnt House and Herodian street collapse, Jerusalem
sources.note: Burn layers, a spear and fallen Temple Mount stones from AD 70.

sources.name: Iudaea Capta coinage
sources.note: Vespasian's victory coins.

views: Josephus's casualty figures are widely considered exaggerated.
Daniel 9:26 ('shall destroy the city and the sanctuary') is read by many traditional interpreters as AD 70; critical scholars read it of Antiochus IV in 167 BC.

395.summary: On Theodosius I's death in 395, the empire was permanently divided between his sons Arcadius (East) and Honorius (West).

sources.name: Zosimus, New History 4.59–5.1; Orosius 7.36
sources.note: Accounts of the succession.

sources.name: Notitia Dignitatum (c. 400)
sources.note: An administrative list showing separate Eastern and Western commands.

views: Earlier splits existed (the Tetrarchy, AD 293); 395 is when the division became lasting.
Many traditional interpreters read the two iron legs as East and West. Others see the legs as a pair without a specific meaning.

476.summary: Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus in 476 and sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople. The date is symbolic: the West had already split into kingdoms.

sources.name: Anonymus Valesianus 8.38; Jordanes, Getica 46; Marcellinus Comes
sources.note: Report the deposition. Marcellinus (6th century) first frames 476 as the end of the Western Empire.

sources.name: Malchus fr. 14
sources.note: The Senate's embassy to Zeno saying one emperor was enough.

views: Julius Nepos, recognised by the East, claimed the title until 480; 480 is another possible end date.
Historians debate 'fall' versus 'transformation' (e.g. Ward-Perkins vs Brown).
The iron-and-clay feet are read as the fragmented kingdoms of Europe (traditional), the Ptolemaic–Seleucid marriages of Daniel 11:6, 17 (critical), or an end-time power still to come (futurist).
